seo.title: Karmic tail 9 3 21 compatibility: The Hermit, The Empress, The World
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 3 21 compatibility: why Waite describes these cards in the words of one garden, and what Paradise Lost says about the couple's main task.

title: Karmic tail 9-3-21 in compatibility: a paradise for two and a whole world beyond the gate
short: The karmic tail 9-3-21 in a couple's matrix is The Hermit, The Empress and The World, and Waite describes these cards in the words of a single story: a garden for two, its threshold and the world beyond the gate. The couple enters the task wanting solitude together, lives it by growing a shared home and a shared work, and its main task is not to lock itself inside its own paradise but to carry that paradise out into the wider world.

sections.h2: The evidence in Waite: a garden, a threshold and a world
paragraphs: Arthur Edward Waite published The Pictorial Key to the Tarot in 1910, together with the deck drawn by Pamela Colman Smith. His numbers for these cards are the same as on the site, and he describes four of them in the words of one biblical story.

**The Empress** is "the inferior Garden of Eden, the Earthly Paradise, all that is symbolized by the visible house of man". A field of corn ripens before her; beyond, there is a fall of water. In the 9-3-21 tail the garden stands in the middle of the road.

**The Lovers** Waite drew as Adam and Eve, "when they first occupied the paradise of the earthly body": behind the man the Tree of Life, behind the woman the Tree of Knowledge with the serpent twining round it. On **The Devil** the same two appear, "as if Adam and Eve after the Fall", chained to a ring before the altar: "Hereof is the chain and fatality of the material life." Wen notices a detail: the woman's tail on The Devil bears fruit, and "the fruit on her tail is a reminder of why the pair of lovers are now here chained". These two cards are the centre of the 9-3-21 couple: The Devil for 89.6% of couples, The Lovers for 10.4%. The atmosphere of such a couple is either Eden before the fruit or its threshold after.

Waite saves the main point about The Devil for the end of his description: the card signifies "the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden when those are driven forth therefrom who have eaten the forbidden fruit". The Dweller of the Threshold comes from Edward Bulwer-Lytton's novel Zanoni (1842), where it is the horror that meets a pupil at the threshold of initiation when he steps there unprepared. And one more sentence from Waite: the one exalted above the chained pair "is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman".

**The World** in Waite is a garden again. In the first part of his book it is "the soul's intoxication in the earthly paradise, but still guarded by the Divine Watchers" — the four living creatures of Ezekiel's vision and the Apocalypse. Ezekiel himself says who they are: "and I knew that they were the cherubims" (Ezekiel 10:20). It is cherubims, with a flaming sword, that God places "at the east of the garden of Eden", "to keep the way of the tree of life" (Genesis 3:24). The watchers around the dancing figure of The World are of the same kind as the guard at Eden's gate. In the second part Waite adds that The World is "perhaps more especially a story of the past, referring to that day when all was declared to be good", and also "the state of the restored world". One card holds both the garden that was lost and the one still to be found.

**The Hermit** is the only one of these cards without a garden. An old man with a lantern and a staff stands on a height; Waite sees in him a blend of "the Ancient of Days with the Light of the World" and calls it a card of attainment. It is a figure of the road.

Laid out in the couple's order, the cards tell one thing: two people on a desert road (9), a garden (3), the garden's threshold at the centre (15) and the world beyond the gate (21). This is our reading — Waite wrote nothing about the tails of the matrix. But the words are his.

sections.h2: Paradise Lost: a marriage from the bower to the gate
paragraphs: Milton composed the poem when he was already blind and dictated it to helpers; Paradise Lost came out in 1667, and its sequel, Paradise Regained, in 1671. God and Satan, angels and devils act in the poem, but its human middle is a marriage. Milton takes one couple through everything: a secluded bower, work in the garden, a guest at table, a quarrel about working apart, the fruit, mutual reproach, reconciliation and the walk out through the gate.

He knew marriage first-hand. In 1642 Milton married the young Mary Powell; soon afterwards she went back to her parents and returned only in 1645. In those years he wrote The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce (1643), where he named the chief end of marriage "a meet and happy conversation". In his day conversation meant not only talk but a whole shared life. For Lisovskaya, the entry to a couple's task is its "common language" and shared wishes. Milton thought a common language was the point of marriage.
Next come the cards of the tail and the couple's centre, book by book. Quotations follow Milton's text in modern spelling; references give book and line.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Hermit: "solitude sometimes is best society"
paragraphs: In Book IV Adam and Eve walk through the garden: "So hand in hand they passed". At nightfall they go to their bower, and Milton takes care to say: "Other creature here, / Bird, beast, insect, or worm, durst enter none, / Such was their awe of Man." Not even nymphs and fauns slept in a bower "more sacred and sequestered". This is the entry of the 9-3-21 couple: the wish for a world for two that nobody enters uninvited. Such couples recognise themselves by small things. A language of half-words. Evenings without guests. Decisions their friends hear about once everything is done. The feeling that together they need nobody.

But The Hermit at the entry is also the right to be alone inside the couple. Milton gives it to Adam in Book IX. Eve suggests they work apart, and Adam, hesitating, agrees: "For solitude sometimes is best society, / And short retirement urges sweet return" (IX, 249–250). Lisovskaya describes The Hermit in a couple the same way: each has a time and a place to be alone, love shows in deeds, and every step — from the first kiss to the wedding — is taken slowly. A short retreat for the sake of a sweet return is the good form of this card.

The word solitude comes back in the poem with another meaning. On the evening after the fruit, God walks into the garden and does not find the couple: "Where art thou, Adam, wont with joy to meet / My coming seen far off? I miss thee here, / Not pleased, thus entertained with solitude" (X, 103–105). The two have hidden "among / The thickest trees", and the one who came to them is left alone. This is the shadow of the entry: solitude for two has become a hiding place, and the one left lonely is the one not let in.

Waite's divinatory list for The Hermit reversed reads like a retelling of the third chapter of Genesis: "Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution." Disguise is the fig leaves the two sewed together to make "themselves aprons". Concealment: "Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden". Fear is Adam's answer: "I heard thee in the garden, and of thy voice / Afraid, being naked, hid myself" (X, 116–117). Milton does not believe in the disguise: "vain covering, if to hide / Their guilt and dreaded shame!" (IX, 1113–1114).

The Hermit also has knowledge gained alone. Wen writes that, reversed, this card is a person who "prefers to rely on his or her own mistakes and experience than to learn from others". Eve, having picked the fruit by herself, thanks exactly that: "Experience, next, to thee I owe, / Best guide" (IX, 807–808). And her very first thought after the new knowledge is to keep it hidden: "And I perhaps am secret".

In a couple's life this looks ordinary. One is stuck at work and says nothing about it for a month. The other has had bad news and decided not to "burden" anyone with it. Both agree that family and friends need not know about the quarrel. Lisovskaya names The Hermit's minus in a couple directly: problems pile up in silence, each lives on their own, being together is uncomfortable but being alone is frightening. The entry to the task is always double: the same quiet that protects the union one day starts to hide it.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Empress: a garden that grows faster than two pairs of hands
paragraphs: The middle of the tail shows how the couple walks from wish to task. In 9-3-21 it is The Empress: fertility, abundance, growth. Lisovskaya sees in it family and marriage, a shared business, a move closer to nature, learning to handle money as a family, children if there are or will be any. In Milton she is the garden itself and the table.

In Book V a guest comes to the couple — the archangel Raphael. Eve lays a table on a mound of turf, piled with all the gifts of autumn, "though spring and autumn here / Danced hand in hand" (V, 394–395). Raphael greets the hostess with words in which The Empress is already looking towards The World: "Hail, Mother of Mankind, whose fruitful womb / Shall fill the world more numerous with thy sons" (V, 388–389). The fertility of the garden promises to fill the whole world: the middle of the tail leads to its end. For a couple, "sons" can be anything two people grow together — a home, a business, pupils, people they have helped.

In Book IX the garden becomes a problem for the first time. Eve tells her husband what any couple with a home and a shared business might say: "till more hands / Aid us, the work under our labour grows, / Luxurious by restraint; what we by day / Lop overgrown, or prune, or prop, or bind, / One night or two with wanton growth derides / Tending to wild" (IX, 207–212). And she proposes: "Let us divide our labours". Her argument is thoroughly modern: when we work side by side, "Looks intervene and smiles, or object new / Casual discourse draw on", and in the evening we sit down to a supper that "comes unearned".

Adam's answer is just as familiar — "For not to irksome toil, but to delight, / He made us" — and only then does he agree to a short parting. The first quarrel of the first couple is not about love but about housekeeping: what matters more, getting things done or being together. This is the middle of the 9-3-21 tail. The Empress's abundance grows and demands hands, and the couple divides the garden: roses for one, ivy for the other. In a modern couple it is one person's renovation and the other's project, the children on a rota, a shared calendar instead of a shared evening. Everything grows, everything works, and the casual talk is put off until the holiday. Lisovskaya names the minus of this card in a couple: rivalry, a lopsided share of chores, "one grows and the other does not", work coming before family.

Milton marks the moment of parting with one gesture: "from her husband's hand her hand / Soft she withdrew" (IX, 385–386). Adam, waiting for her, weaves a garland of flowers "to adorn / Her tresses, and her rural labours crown; / As reapers oft are wont their harvest-queen". This is The Empress quite literally, the queen of the harvest. When Eve comes back with the fruit, "From his slack hand the garland wreathed for Eve / Down dropt, and all the faded roses shed" (IX, 892–893). The garden was the reason to go off to separate corners, and in separate corners the couple met disaster.

Milton does not make the scene simple. Eve is right: "Frail is our happiness, if this be so, / And Eden were no Eden, thus exposed" (IX, 340–341) — a paradise that has to be guarded is no longer paradise. Adam is right too when he lets her go: "Go; for thy stay, not free, absents thee more" (IX, 372). Milton assigns the roles by sex, as the seventeenth century did. In a 9-3-21 couple either partner can be the one who goes off to work alone and the one who lets go.

sections.h2: The couple's atmosphere — The Devil: the guard at the garden's exit
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is its atmosphere, what happens between two people when nobody is watching. For 89.6% of couples with the 9-3-21 tail it is The Devil, a card that never appears in the centre of a personal matrix for any date. This centre arises only when there are two. So it is in Milton: Satan comes to Eden for the sake of the couple.

Watching them embrace, Satan says, "Sight hateful, sight tormenting!" — and what he envies is not the garden but the two of them. The original is sharper than any translation: "thus these two, / Imparadised in one another's arms, / The happier Eden" (IV, 505–507). The Devil is the first to understand that this couple's paradise is not a place but what lies between them. He himself carries the opposite inside: "myself am Hell" (IV, 75).

After the fruit Milton hardly needs Satan: from here on The Devil grows out of love itself. Eve, having eaten, wonders whether to share with her husband or rather "keep the odds of knowledge in my power / Without copartner? … the more to draw his love, / And render me more equal; and perhaps, / A thing not undesirable, sometime / Superior". And she sums up with a line that describes centre 15 better than any treatise: "for, inferior, who is free?" (IX, 820–825). A minute later jealousy stops her: if she dies, there will be "Adam, wedded to another Eve". The decision is made — share the fruit, because "without him" she could "live no life".

Adam chooses the same way, out of fear of loss: "I feel / The link of Nature draw me", "for what thou art is mine… to lose thee were to lose myself" (IX, 913–914, 957–959). A link, "what thou art is mine", losing the other means losing oneself: the chain Waite writes of is woven here out of tenderness. Lisovskaya describes The Devil in a couple's atmosphere in the same terms without the poetry: the wish to own the partner, jealousy, control, attempts to hold the other through intimacy, money or status, silence about one's own desires. Her final thought about this energy is that nobody belongs to anybody. On weekdays it looks smaller than in Milton: whoever earns more makes the decisions; an evening with friends without the partner sounds like betrayal; good news is first checked for whether it might give the other an advantage.

The end of Book IX is an exact picture of how such an atmosphere eats time: "Thus they in mutual accusation spent / The fruitless hours, but neither self-condemning; / And of their vain contest appeared no end" (IX, 1187–1189). Milton shows the way out in Book X, and it is not finding someone to blame. Eve speaks first: "Between us two let there be peace" (X, 924). Adam answers: "let us no more contend, nor blame / Each other, blamed enough elsewhere; but strive / In offices of love, how we may lighten / Each other's burden" (X, 958–961). The striving remains, but now the two compete not over who stands higher but over who can lighten the other's load. This is the strong version of centre 15: passion, attachment and a readiness to accept each other's dark sides — without any right of ownership.

Waite leaves this card a hope: the one exalted above the chained pair "is not to be their master for ever". If control in a couple has stopped being a metaphor and become fear for one's safety, that is a reason to talk to a psychologist, and in danger to call a local emergency number.

For 10.4% of couples the centre is The Lovers — the same Adam and Eve, but before the fruit. Wen writes of this card: "there is a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning", and right away recalls the saying "under every flower a serpent coiled". For these couples the atmosphere is being in love and choosing; Lisovskaya sees its minus in idealising the relationship and in perfectionism. The arithmetic is the same for both centres: 21 + 15 = 36 → 9 and 21 + 6 = 27 → 9. The main task added to the atmosphere brings the couple back to the entry.

sections.h2: Main task — The World: "The world was all before them"
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is D, and Lisovskaya reads it mostly through its minus: what the couple fails at and has to learn. The World in its minus, for her, is a closed, unwelcoming couple with a Groundhog Day routine, a ban on friends and family, a fear of change and the rule "old is better than new". For The World reversed Waite gives four words: "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence."

Milton gave this minus to Eve in Book XI, when the couple learns that the garden must be left. There is no better speech about attachment to a place in the whole poem: "Must I thus leave thee Paradise? thus leave / Thee, native soil! … O flowers, / That never will in other climate grow" (XI, 269–274). The flowers she named herself, the nuptial bower she adorned herself — everything The Empress has grown holds her in place. The archangel Michael's answer is one of the most exact formulas of The World as a task: "nor set thy heart, / Thus over-fond, on that which is not thine" (XI, 288–289).

In a 9-3-21 couple it looks like this. A house built with their own hands becomes the reason not to move when it is time. The circle of two lets in no new people. The holiday is in the same place every year, because "it's nice there". A job offer in another city is turned down without a conversation. The garden has grown, and its walls have become the horizon.

The World upright Waite describes in the words of the road: "Assured success, recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place." Adam and Eve are the first emigrants, and Milton does not make their leaving a mere punishment. Before they go, Michael leads Adam up a hill "Of Paradise the highest; from whose top / The hemisphere of earth, in clearest ken, / Stretched out to the amplest reach of prospect lay" (XI, 377–380). Lisovskaya sees in The World's plus couples who travel and move a lot, live between cultures, accept each other wholly and agree on a shared philosophy of life.

Michael's last words answer the whole tail: "then wilt thou not be loth / To leave this Paradise, but shalt possess / A Paradise within thee, happier far" (XII, 585–587). The paradise within is The Empress's garden carried to where The Hermit lives. And straight after: "Let us descend now therefore from this top / Of speculation" (XII, 588–589). Light found at the top has to be carried down. In Book VIII Raphael advised the couple: "Dream not of other worlds". At the end of Book XII a whole world lies before them.

Eve answers in her own way: "with thee to go, / Is to stay here; without thee here to stay, / Is to go hence unwilling; thou to me / Art all things under Heaven, all places thou" (XII, 615–618). This is the strong version of The World: home moves to wherever the other is. But the same sentence hides a risk that leads back to the couple's centre. If the other is all places, the world shrinks to two again, and a new fence grows round them. The task of The World is wider than the partner: to go out to people together, not to replace people with each other. Michael tells Eve: "Where he abides, think there thy native soil" (XI, 292). In Milton this is said to a wife about her husband; in a 9-3-21 couple it holds for both of them about each other.

sections.h2: The poem's last line leads back to the first card
paragraphs: "The world was all before them, where to choose / Their place of rest, and Providence their guide: / They, hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow, / Through Eden took their solitary way" (XII, 646–649). The World — the main task — is named outright. After it comes a choice of where to live, a word belonging to The Lovers. And the last word is the hermit's road. The 9-3-21 tail closes into a ring, and the numbers show it just as clearly: 21 + 15 = 36 → 9. The main task added to the couple's atmosphere gives the entry. Having gone out into the world, the two are again alone together on the road — with the same Hermit, but a different one.

Milton marks the couple's whole journey with one gesture. In Book IV they walk through the garden "hand in hand" (IV, 321) and go the same way to their bower (IV, 689). On the morning of the quarrel Eve draws her hand away (IX, 385–386). After the fruit Adam takes her hand differently: "Her hand he seized" (IX, 1037; the standard Russian translation softens it to "led her by the hand"). At the gate the archangel leads both out: "In either hand the hastening Angel caught / Our lingering parents" (XII, 637–638). And the last line is "hand in hand" once more. The same two hands and the same road for two; what has changed is the meaning of solitude. At the start it was a refuge from the world; at the end it became a road through it.

There is a second sum too: 9 + 21 = 30 → 3. The couple's middle is calculated differently — by adding the middles of the two personal tails — but here it matches the sum of the two ends. The Empress's garden is made of solitude and the whole world. Without either it does not grow: solitude alone turns the garden into a wall, the world alone into a thoroughfare.

sections.h2: What the numbers of the compatibility matrix record
paragraphs: The 9-3-21 tail occurs in about one couple in 295 (0.339%) and ranks 68th of the 97 couple tails. Running through every date since 1900 shows what it is made of, and these numbers continue the same plot.

ul: **One brings The World, the other The Devil.** In 89.6% of these couples the partners' personal tails are 15-20-5 and 21-10-16, and these are exactly the couples with The Devil in the centre. One enters their own tail through The Devil, the other through The World, and the couple's entry is their sum: 15 + 21 = 36 → 9. The couple's two strongest cards, the main task and the centre, stand at the start of two different people's personal tails.

**Neither partner has The Hermit.** In none of the three combinations — 15-20-5 + 21-10-16, 3-13-10 + 6-17-11 (8%), 21-10-7 + 6-20-14 (2%) — does a nine appear in the partners' personal tails. This couple's Hermit is always born of the two: a solitude neither had on their own.

**The World is almost always already in hand.** In 91.6% of couples one partner begins their personal tail with The World. What is the main task for the couple is, for one of the two, the entry to their own tail.
**The Devil exists only in couples.** A centre of 15 never occurs in a personal matrix. In these couples it is always made of the personal centres 5 and 10 — The Hierophant and The Wheel of Fortune.

**The couple's World is never folded.** The main task is always an exact sum: 16 + 5 for 89.6% of couples (one partner's Tower and the other's Hierophant), 10 + 11 for 8.4%, 7 + 14 for 2%. Collapse and teaching give The World — in Milton, after the Fall, the last two books are taken up by the archangel's lesson (our reading).

sections.h2: The couple's values: the hill and the dream
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, what the union exists for. For 69.1% of 9-3-21 couples it is The Hermit again, for 30.9% The Moon. The split depends on the centre: with The Devil, The Hermit stands in the values of 75.6% of couples; with The Lovers, The Moon does for 86%.

Milton supplies a scene here too. Before the expulsion Michael tells Adam: "Ascend / This hill; let Eve (for I have drenched her eyes) / Here sleep below; while thou to foresight wakest; / As once thou sleptst, while she to life was formed" (XI, 366–369). One looks at the world from the summit; the other learns the same in a dream. When Adam comes down, Eve greets him: "Whence thou returnest, and whither wentest, I know; / For God is also in sleep; and dreams advise" (XII, 610–611).

The Hermit in the values is knowledge from a height: the couple treasures understanding, serious conversation, the light each has found alone and brought to the other. The Moon in the values is knowledge without proof: sensitivity, intuition, understanding without words. Lisovskaya advises couples with The Moon to accept a partner's need to withdraw sometimes — it is a way to recover, not a lack of love. The advice almost repeats the entry of this tail word for word. In Milton the hill goes to the husband and the dream to the wife; in 9-3-21 couples the values are shared, and the card does not say which of the two climbs the hill.

Every point of the couple is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, folded to 22. The date 06.03.1978 has the personal tail 21-10-16 and centre 5; the date 17.01.1976 has the tail 15-20-5 and centre 10.

Here the couple's middle is calculated from the partners' middles, not from the ends of the tail, although 9 + 21 also gives 3. This is the most common combination: one partner with The World at the start of the personal tail, the other with The Devil.

In this couple The Hermit stands on six more points. "What fills the union" is 9 + 18 = 27 → 9. The whole "Relationship and common language" line is 9-9-9, and so is the whole "The couple's money" line. "The couple's values" is 9. Seven nines in one compatibility matrix are rare: it happens in about 2.5% of couples with this tail. Their "Image of the couple" is The Hierophant (6 + 17 = 23 → 5), and "What to create together" is The Emperor (3 + 1 = 4).

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: a paradise you can carry
paragraphs: More than two hundred years after Milton, Mark Twain retold the same story as a comedy. Extracts from Adam's Diary (1904) opens squarely with The Hermit: "This new creature with the long hair is a good deal in the way. It is always hanging around and following me about. I don't like this; I am not used to company." Adam builds himself a shelter against the rain, but "could not have it to myself in peace. The new creature intruded." Later he runs away, builds another shelter "in a secluded place", covers his tracks — and promises to "emigrate again, when occasion offers". The Hermit and The World in two comic entries.

The last entry of the diary is headed "Ten Years Later": "it is better to live outside the Garden with her than inside it without her." And Eve's Diary (1905) closes with one line from Adam at her grave: "Wheresoever she was, there was Eden." This is The World solved by a 9-3-21 couple: a paradise that cannot be locked up but can be carried along.
What changes the script can be read in the poem itself:

ul: **Solitude short, and with a return.** "Solitude sometimes is best society" as long as "short retirement urges sweet return". A hiding place where the other is not expected is already the thicket where they hid from the voice.
**Divide the garden, but meet by evening.** Dividing the work is sensible; going off to separate corners and not telling each other what grew in each is how the couple met disaster.
**Be the first to say "let there be peace".** In Milton the way out of mutual reproach starts not with finding the guilty one but with two people competing to lighten each other's load.

**Open the gate.** Guests, friends, the road, new people, a move if it is needed. Michael leads the couple out through the gate, but from there they walk on their own: "where to choose / Their place of rest".
**Do not make the other "all places".** Home can be carried to wherever the other is. The world cannot be replaced by a partner.

intro: The oddity shows at once. The Hermit is a card of one person, yet here it stands at the entry to a task shared by two. Waite calls The Empress "the inferior Garden of Eden, the Earthly Paradise". His World is "a story of the past", the day "when all was declared to be good", and at the same time "the restored world". And in the centre of the matrix of 89.6% of these couples stands The Devil, about whom Waite is most precise of all: the card signifies "the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden when those are driven forth therefrom who have eaten the forbidden fruit".

A garden, its threshold, the world beyond it and a lonely road: this is the story of Adam and Eve. John Milton told it in full, as the story of a marriage, in Paradise Lost (1667). The poem ends: "They, hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow, / Through Eden took their solitary way." The word hermit comes from the Greek erēmitēs, "a person of the desert", and the standard Russian translation by Arkady Steinberg renders that last line with pustynnoyu, "desert", the same root as pustynnik, the old Russian word for a hermit. The poem about the first couple ends on the first card of this tail.
The three roles of these cards in the couple's tail, in brief:

ul: **9 · The Hermit — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: a quiet world of its own that outsiders do not enter, long conversations, the right of each to be alone sometimes. The same entry turns into resistance when solitude becomes a hiding place, from other people and from each other.

**3 · The Empress — middle of the task.** How the couple walks the path: it grows a shared garden — a home, a work, prosperity, children if there are or will be any. The garden grows faster than two people can keep up, and one day each goes off to work in a corner of their own.

**21 · The World — main task.** To go out through the gate: open the union to people, to the road and to change, and not turn paradise into a fortress. This point is read above all through its minus — closedness, stagnation, fear of change — and it shows what the couple has to learn.

intro: This is not a forecast and not a verdict. The tail describes a plot that every couple lives in its own way. What follows is the evidence: what Waite, Benebell Wen and Yuliana Lisovskaya write, what the numbers of the compatibility matrix show, and how this story sounds in verse.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-3-21 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task written in three cards. The entry is The Hermit: the two want a quiet world of their own and the right to be alone sometimes. The middle is The Empress: the couple grows a shared home, work and prosperity. The main task is The World: not to lock themselves in their own paradise but to open the union to people, the road and change. The plot of the tail is the story of Adam and Eve, told by Milton in Paradise Lost.

faq.q: Is 9-3-21 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events or pass a verdict. Lisovskaya reads the main task through its minus, so it shows above all where the couple struggles: closedness, fear of change, attachment to a place and to each other. The strong version of the same tail is a couple that knows how to withdraw and come back, grows something shared and takes it out into the world.

faq.q: How is the couple tail 9-3-21 different from the personal tail 9-3-21?
faq.a: They are different calculations with different roles for the points. A couple's tail is the sum of the points of two personal matrices, and its entry, middle and main task describe a task shared by two. The personal tail 9-3-21 occurs for 1,250 dates since 1900 and speaks about one person; the site has a separate article about it. The same numbers do not carry one reading over to the other.

faq.q: How is the couple tail 9-21-3 different?
faq.a: It has the same cards in another order: The World stands in the middle and The Empress becomes the main task. Such a couple walks its path through the road and change, and what it has to learn is home, fertility and growing something shared. The 9-21-3 tail is far rarer — about 0.023% of couples — and every such couple has The Lovers in the centre.

faq.q: Why do these couples almost always have The Devil in the centre?
faq.a: For 89.6% of couples with the 9-3-21 tail the centre is 15, and it is always made of the personal centres 5 and 10. A personal matrix never has 15 in the centre, so this atmosphere appears only between two people. Waite calls The Devil "the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden": the attachment and fear of loss that stand at the exit of a shared paradise. The remaining 10.4% of couples have The Lovers in the centre.

report: The poem about the first couple in the world ends on the very card with which a 9-3-21 couple begins its shared task. The last lines of Milton's Paradise Lost: "They, hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow, / Through Eden took their solitary way." The word hermit comes from the Greek erēmitēs, "a person of the desert", and the standard Russian translation renders that solitary way with pustynnoyu, "desert", the root of pustynnik, the old Russian word for a hermit.

The coincidence would be merely amusing if it were not for Waite. He calls The Empress "the inferior Garden of Eden, the Earthly Paradise". The World is "a story of the past", the day "when all was declared to be good", and also "the restored world". And of The Devil, which most often stands in the centre of such couples, he writes that the card signifies "the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden when those are driven forth therefrom who have eaten the forbidden fruit". A road, a garden, a threshold and a world beyond the gate: **the story of Adam and Eve, laid out across the cards of the tail**. Waite wrote nothing about tails; this is a reading. But the words are his.

report.h3: Solitude that easily turns into a hiding place

report: The entry to the task is The Hermit: what the two want together. In Milton it is the bower where "Bird, beast, insect, or worm, durst enter none". A language of half-words, evenings without guests, decisions friends hear about once everything is done. And the right of each to be alone sometimes: "For solitude sometimes is best society, / And short retirement urges sweet return."

The word solitude comes back in the poem. After the fruit, God walks into the garden and the couple is gone: the two have hidden "among / The thickest trees", and the one who came to them is left "entertained with solitude". Waite's Hermit reversed is "Concealment, disguise… fear" — almost a retelling of the third chapter of Genesis, with its fig leaves, the trees of the garden and Adam's answer, "Afraid, being naked, hid myself". In life it is ordinary: one says nothing for a month about trouble at work, the other has decided not to "burden" anyone. **The same quiet that protects the union one day starts to hide it.**

report.h3: A garden that grows faster than two pairs of hands

report: The middle of the task is The Empress: a home, a work, prosperity, everything two people grow together. In Book IX the garden becomes a problem for the first time. Eve says what any couple with a home and a shared business might say: whatever "we by day / Lop overgrown, or prune, or prop, or bind, / One night or two with wanton growth derides / Tending to wild". And she proposes: "Let us divide our labours", because side by side they only exchange smiles, and supper "comes unearned". Adam objects — "For not to irksome toil, but to delight, / He made us" — and still lets her go.

The first quarrel of the first couple is not about love but about housekeeping. Today it is one person's renovation and the other's project, a shared calendar instead of a shared evening. Milton marks the moment with a gesture: "from her husband's hand her hand / Soft she withdrew". Meanwhile Adam weaves her a garland, as reapers crown their "harvest-queen", and when she comes back with the fruit, "From his slack hand the garland wreathed for Eve / Down dropt". The garden was the reason to go off to separate corners, and in separate corners the couple met disaster.

report.h3: This couple's paradise is not a place but what lies between two

report: The Devil in the centre is the couple's atmosphere, what lies between two people when nobody is watching. Watching Adam and Eve embrace, Milton's Satan sees in them "The happier Eden": he is the first to grasp that this couple's paradise is not the garden.

From there The Devil grows out of love itself. Eve wonders whether to "keep the odds of knowledge in my power / Without copartner", and sums up: "for, inferior, who is free?" Adam chooses out of fear of loss: "for what thou art is mine… to lose thee were to lose myself". The chain is woven from tenderness. On weekdays it looks smaller: whoever earns more makes the decisions, an evening with friends without the partner sounds like betrayal. Lisovskaya reduces this energy to one thought: nobody belongs to anybody.

Then come the hours in which they were "neither self-condemning; / And of their vain contest appeared no end". Milton's way out is not a search for the guilty one. Eve speaks first: "Between us two let there be peace." Adam answers: "but strive / In offices of love, how we may lighten / Each other's burden". **The striving remains, but now the contest is over who can lighten the other's load.** If control in a couple has stopped being a metaphor and become fear for one's safety, that is a reason to talk to a psychologist, and in danger to call a local emergency number or crisis line.

report.h3: A whole world beyond the gate

report: The main task is The World, and it is read above all through its minus: closedness, stagnation, fear of change. In Milton this minus is Eve's lament: "Must I thus leave thee Paradise?" — and her grief for the flowers she named herself. In a 9-3-21 couple it is a house built with their own hands that becomes the reason not to move, a circle of two that lets in no new people. The garden has grown, and its walls have become the horizon. The archangel answers Eve: "nor set thy heart, / Thus over-fond, on that which is not thine", and promises Adam "A Paradise within thee, happier far."

There is a subtle trap as well. Eve tells Adam: "thou to me / Art all things under Heaven, all places thou". That is beautiful as long as home moves to wherever the other is. But if the other is all places, the world shrinks to two again. **The task of The World is wider than the partner: to go out to people together, not to replace people with each other.**

Milton marks the couple's whole journey with a hand: "hand in hand" in the garden, the hand withdrawn on the morning of the quarrel, the hand that after the fruit "he seized", and "hand in hand" again on the road. The same two people and the same solitary way — what has changed is the meaning of solitude. At the start it was a refuge from the world; at the end it became a road through it.

Mark Twain retold this story as a comedy, and in the entry headed "Ten Years Later" his Adam admits: "it is better to live outside the Garden with her than inside it without her." At Eve's grave he will say: "Wheresoever she was, there was Eden." This is the strong version of the 9-3-21 tail: **a paradise that cannot be locked up but can be carried along.**
